changes: # AfterFix: Evaluating Data Recovery After a Correct Code Patch
Agents receive a correct patch, complete evidence and permission to rebuild derived tables.
A later CPU check reveals an important limitation: removing filters from the supplied patches solves all 24 cases. The tasks therefore test adaptation of existing repair logic.
We present these findings as a small, controlled study, with clear limits on task difficulty and production relevance.
given correct application SQL and explicit recovery requirements

Our contribution is an inspectable task set and controlled evaluation. Every supplied patch contains reconstruction logic exposed by removing work filters. This limits the task to adapting existing logic.
They cover acknowledgements, reservations, object versions, delegated access, event ordering and decisions based on available evidence. All cases are authored examples.
These show solutions and rejection of selected mistakes. The same authors wrote cases and oracles; separate implementations are not independent human review.
The variants are not additional model runs. Development cases were excluded from the original evaluation, but the authors knew the test cases.
An edge declares that one table or concept depends on another.
It returns existing nodes, edges and evidence references. It supplies no private information, does not identify damaged rows and does not plan repairs.
The larger model performs better overall but not on every case.
The measured finding is that execution and stability checks do not separate correct from incorrect generated repairs in these runs. Displayed rows provide evidence, not a correctness verdict.
AfterFix starts with damaged projections and supplied correct SQL.
Original, corrected H08, v3, scope-diagnostic and review evidence remain separate. Earlier drafts, package v1 and original results are preserved. Public hosting and licensing remain pending.
